Then solve a fresh version that changes a binding constraint and explain why the original recommendation changes or survives.

All examination cases and proofs are original and synthetic. Scoped method context reuses the accepted Saez incidence notes, Angrist schooling notes and Saez social-insurance notes. Other arguments are finite specializations of methods taught and linked in the twelve accepted or review-stage chapter packages; no new empirical, legal or whole-paper verification is claimed.

Integrative project — a funded local opportunity program under disputed effects

Build and defend a finite policy laboratory connecting public finance, labor opportunities, housing and service capacity, environmental costs, distribution and causal identification. Every person, observation, technology and institutional rule below is synthetic. The exercise supplies a completely specified decision problem; it does not estimate an actual city's treatment effects or recommend a real program. Use Chapters1–12 to question the assumptions as well as solve the model.

Work individually first, then conduct an adversarial review. Suggested effort is10–14hours with open resources and a standard-library Python interpreter. Timing, the100-point rubric and the85-point advancement threshold are authored, uncalibrated study choices. Require at least15/20in every domain, repair any critical accounting or identification error, and complete an oral transfer before advancement. A high score is not institutional certification.

Download the five-file offline capsule: synthetic inputs, benchmark analysis, complete output, payload manifest, and reproduction guide. Keep the basenames together. The output exposes every feasible policy/state account and every infeasibility diagnostic, not merely the preferred policy. Your submission must include your own implementation or independently reconstructible workbook, seven task answers, and a two-page decision memo distinguishing assumptions, evidence and judgments.

Population, choices and real resources

There are four atomless household groups, each of mass one: P1,P2,R1,R2, in that fixed priority order. Think of four continua of small households, not four strategic players. Their baseline real output accrues as income, with no omitted employer loss: incomes are(20,20,30,30). Every household owns its baseline output and consumes numeraire. It can apply for an optional service-linked work opportunity. If admitted, its additional real production is θ+vᵢ, credited entirely to its income; travel consumes one real good. Offsets v=(3,2,1,0) are assumed known, not estimated. These additional outputs do not reduce anyone else's production. There is no labor disutility, commuting congestion or external employer profit beyond the costs stated here.

Program participants need one capacity unit each. The authority chooses capacity k∈{0,1,2,3}, fee f∈{0,1,2}, subsidy s∈{0,1}, and abatement a∈{0,1}. For k=0only(f,s,a)=(0,0,0)is allowed; this is the outside policy. For positive k all combinations enter the candidate menu. One program capacity unit costs two real goods regardless of utilization; administration costs one per admitted participant. Abatement costs one real good if installed, and reduces each participant's emissions from one to one quarter. Idle capacity is not resold in this one-period comparison.

Participants pay f and receive s. Every infinitesimal household takes aggregate environmental harm and the common fiscal refund as fixed when deciding to apply. It applies iff θ+vᵢ−1−f+s≥0, accepting exact indifference by convention. Applicants are admitted in listed-group priority until k units fill; if fewer apply, capacity remains unused. All members of a group have identical primitives; integral capacities and unit group masses make whole-group allocations possible. A denied household cannot purchase another group's slot or change its priority. An admitted household cannot lose money relative to not applying at the same aggregate prices and transfers. Nevertheless, a nonparticipant can be worse off under the policy than under no program because it pays taxes and suffers pollution. Participation is not a Pareto test.

The groups' shares of total environmental damage are h=(1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8), summing to one. If m households participate, emissions E=m(1−3a/4) cause a real consumption loss dE, allocated hᵢdE. This is a stipulated linear loss in goods, not a health estimate or a monetary value assigned to an observed life. It occurs after program output is available. Weighted evaluation assigns weightsω=(2,2,1,1)to changes in group consumption; the separate unweighted resource calculation gives every good the same weight.

The compact primitive record is (income;offset;damage share;weight)=((20,20,30,30),(3,2,1,0),(1/2,1/4,1/8,1/8),(2,2,1,1)). Technology and policy bounds are (capacity cost,administration,travel,abatement cost,emissions,reduction,reserve limit)=(2,1,1,1,1,3/4,10). There is no endogenous housing rent, migration or electoral contest in this laboratory. Priority assignment and construction cost replace those mechanisms explicitly; the urban and political chapters explain why such omissions matter for transport.

Timing, treasury and feasibility

First the authority commits to a policy before learning θor d. It raises a reserve R=k(3+s)+a through an equal levy ℓ=R/4. It may collect at most10in total. This deliberately conservative reserve covers capacity, abatement, administration and subsidies if every slot fills; anticipated user fees do not relax the initial borrowing prohibition. Fees and subsidies are settled at admission before new output is received. Initial cash after the levy must be nonnegative and sufficient for a nonnegative net user charge max(f−s,0). The supplied incomes satisfy these liquidity restrictions for every policy within the reserve limit.

Second the state is revealed to households; their productivity response and applications occur, then capacity priority determines admission. The authority incurs real public cost C=2k+m+a and cash expenses C+sm, collects fm, and refunds the entire unused balance R+fm−C−sm equally across all four groups. Let b=(R+fm−C−sm)/4. The reserve formula ensures b≥0 because the residual is(1+s)(k−m)+fm. There is no retained treasury profit or unrecorded deficit. Output, travel and environmental loss are then realized. Final consumption must be nonnegative in every decision state.

With zᵢ∈{0,1}indicating admission, final consumption is cᵢ=yᵢ+zᵢ(θ+vᵢ−1−f+s)−ℓ+b−hᵢdE. The benchmark tests reserve, cash, capacity, treasury balance and final consumption separately. A syntactically valid but unfunded policy returns an infeasibility record; it is never treated as a zero-welfare policy. Uniform feasibility means the policy is feasible in every listed state and is required before expected or robust optimization. This uses one common comparison set for state frontiers and regrets.

For example k=3,s=1,a=1requires R=13even at a high fee. It is inadmissible under the reserve limit10; a fee receipt later in the period cannot repair prohibited initial borrowing. There are37candidate policies and31uniformly feasible ones. The six exclusions are precisely k=3,s=1with either abatement choice and any fee. Their reserves are12or13. The smallest final consumption over all feasible policy/state/group combinations is29/2.

Synthetic moments, heldout fit and decision states

A separate synthetic observational cohort supplies untreated and treated conditional means. At covariate x=0the means are8and12; at the heldout x=2they are10and14. A candidate conditional model is μ₀(x)=8+x and μ₁(x)=8+x+θ+B, where B is selection into treatment. Calibration uses only x=0; the x=2cell is held out until the prediction rule is fixed. Thus calibration identifies θ+B=4. The heldout means check extrapolation of the baseline relationship, but do not separately identifyθandB. These are supplied population moments with no sampling uncertainty; creating fictitious standard errors would add information the input does not contain.

Impose the sensitivity restriction B∈[1,3]. Then the sharp causal interval is θ∈[1,3]: every θin that interval is paired with B=4−θand matches all four means. No value outside it can both fit the treated difference and obey the bound. The choice to transport the sameθto the program groups and add their known offsets is a structural assumption. The observational cohort does not establish it.

For the finite decision exercise only, retain θ∈{1,2,3}and d∈{2,4}, independently. Assign effect weights(5/8,1/4,1/8)and damage weights(1/2,1/2). These subjective forecast weights and the finite support are supplied decision assumptions, not probabilities identified by the means. Robust optimization ignores their magnitudes but retains their support. It is robust over these six states only; claiming robustness over everyθ∈[1,3]would require checking application thresholds between the grid points. The state order is(T1D2,T1D4,T2D2,T2D4,T3D2,T3D4), with weights (5/16,5/16,1/8,1/8,1/16,1/16).

Three models(θ,B)=(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)fit training and heldout treated means exactly. A competing slope-two baseline8+2xalso fits training but predicts heldout untreated12and treated16, both too high by2. That failure rejects this particular extrapolation; passing the heldout check does not validate exclusion or remove selection. Keep prediction performance, causal identification and normative decision weights in separate columns.

Seven project tasks

  1. Reconstruct the evidence exercise without using policy outputs. Give all three stated models' training and heldout predictions, derive the full sharp causal interval under B∈[1,3], and diagnose the slope-two model. Label each program primitive as observed synthetic evidence, structural assumption, sensitivity restriction or normative choice. Explain why these categories cannot be pooled into one goodness-of-fit score.
  2. Write the household application and priority-allocation algorithm. Prove that it yields the unique admitted group set under the stated tie rule for every candidate policy/state, including no program, excess demand and unused capacity. Derive the reserve and refund identities. Enumerate the complete candidate menu, uniformly feasible set and every reason for exclusion. For(k,f,s,a)=(3,2,0,0), compare admission atθ=1andθ=2; demonstrate an actual participation threshold.
  3. Derive the treasury and consolidated real-resource identities for arbitrary feasible inputs. For policy(2,0,1,1)in state(θ,d)=(1,2), give reserve, levy, applicants/admitted groups, output, travel, emissions, damage, public real cost, subsidies, expenses, fees, refund and all four consumption changes. Reconcile weighted welfare with total resource change and identify losers. Explain why a subsidy is counted in the treasury and group accounts but cancels as an aggregate real resource.
  4. Independently enumerate every feasible policy/state payoff. Define state-optimal weighted welfare, expected weighted welfare and expected resource gain. Report the complete maximizer sets for both ex ante objectives and all six state frontiers. Give the expected-policy and no-program comparisons; show why the expected recommendation is neither an efficiency theorem nor a Pareto improvement. Your submission must include complete machine-readable rows and one manually reconstructed row.
  5. Define regret relative to the uniformly feasible state frontier. Compute every policy's six regrets and maximum regret; find the full minimax-regret set. Compare no program, the expected-weighted choice and the robust choice. Prove finite enumeration establishes a global optimum over the declared menu, including ties, and explain how randomizing policies or expanding the uncertainty support would change the decision problem.
  6. For a separate forecast sensitivity calculation put probabilityqonθ=3and1−qonθ=1, q∈[0,1]; retain the equal damage weights. Derive each policy's affine expected weighted payoff. Find all supporting policy intervals and exact switching values, including ties. Prove the intervals are sharp by intersecting all pairwise affine inequalities. Locate the baseline mean-effect forecast relative to these switches without claiming the two forecasts have identical distributions or regret problems.
  7. Deliver a reproducible audit and decision memo. Demonstrate quiet API execution with unchanged inputs, a successful isolated five-file CLI run, a preserved-protected-file alias rejection, and an economically valid infeasible-policy diagnostic. Explain the independent checks and exact-arithmetic convention. Choose and defend an objective, report group effects and funding, identify two plausible omitted mechanisms and the evidence needed for them, and prespecify a result that would change your recommendation. Separate implementability under the model from real administrative, political and legal feasibility.
Complete instructor solutions and global certificates

1. Fit does not resolve selection

Training untreated prediction is8and treated prediction is8+θ+B=12for all three pairs. Heldout predictions are10and10+θ+B=14. All residuals are zero. Since B=4−θ, the restriction1≤B≤3is equivalent to1≤θ≤3; every point has an admissible matching B, proving both necessity and sufficiency. The numerical evidence check is (identified sum,causal lower,causal upper,heldout treated,wrong-slope treated,error)=(4,1,3,14,16,2). A slope-two model changes the heldout baseline by2while leaving x=0unchanged.

The four cell means are observed within the supplied synthetic evidence. Baseline linear extrapolation, constant selection acrossx, transport ofθto the program, productivity offsets, atomless behavior, priority and technology are model assumptions. The bound on selection and finiteθ/dsupport are sensitivity restrictions; forecast weights are additional decision inputs. Welfare weights and the choice of expected welfare versus regret express evaluative judgments. Forecast probabilities could in principle be informed by evidence, but these inputs do not estimate them. A perfect moment fit cannot determine who deserves a welfare weight of two or make a funding constraint disappear.

2. Choice, rationing and funding

Compute each net participation gain gᵢ=θ+vᵢ−1−f+s. Mark applications where gᵢ≥0. Visit the four groups in fixed order, admitting an applicant iff the current admitted count is belowk. This admits exactlymin(k,number of applicants)groups, all with nonnegative gain. If an alternative admitted set first differs at indexi, it either excludes an eligible priority group while admitting a later group or leaves a slot idle despite an applicant. Both violate the rule. Thus the set is unique, including equality because the rule explicitly accepts a zero gain. Whenk=0no one is admitted even though several would like to join.

For(3,2,0,0),θ=1gives gains(1,0,−1,−2); P1and P2apply and both enter, leaving one slot unused. Atθ=2the gains are(2,1,0,−1); R1also enters. These are genuine behavioral differences, not a welfare formula evaluated at a fixed participant count. Gross reserve is3(3)+0=9in both states. Atθ=1, real expenses are6+2=8, fees4, and total refund5; atθ=2expenses9, fees6, refund6. Hence (participants low,participants middle,reserve,refund low,refund middle)=(2,3,9,5,6).

There is one outside action plus3·3·2·2=36positive-capacity actions. The reserve is k(3+s)+a. Only k3s1violates10: reserves12or13for all three fees, so six fail and31remain. All remaining initial cash and user-charge tests pass. Checking each retained state establishes final consumption at least29/2. The menu certificate is (candidates,feasible,excluded,minimum consumption)=(37,31,6,29/2). A lower fee cannot rescue an initial reserve violation, and a larger fee is not usable before its receipt. Exclusion is an institutional timing restriction, not a negative welfare observation.

3. Every payment has a counterpart

With m=Σzᵢ, treasury receipts are R+fm and expenses plus refunds are C+sm+4b. Their equality defines b. Summing consumption changes cancels−R+4b+(s−f)m=−C. SinceΣhᵢ=1, the consolidated identity isΣΔcᵢ=Σzᵢ(θ+vᵢ)−m−C−dE. Capacity, travel, administration, abatement and damage are real costs. Fees, subsidies, levies and refunds are transfers. This proof is universal for the stated mass-one structure, not a coincidence in one row.

For(2,0,1,1),reserve9and levy9/4fund the full program. All four apply atθ1, but only P1/P2enter. Additional output is4+3=7, travel2, emissions1/2, damage1, real public cost4+2+1=7. Subsidies total2, expenses9, fees0and refund0. Group consumption changes are(5/4,1/2,−19/8,−19/8), giving final consumption(85/4,41/2,221/8,221/8). Both richer groups lose even though the two priority groups gain.

The complete account check is (R,levy,m,output,travel,emissions,damage,C,subsidies,expenses,fees,refund,resource,weighted)=(9,9/4,2,7,2,1/2,1,7,2,9,0,0,-3,-5/4). Total resource change is7−2−7−1=−3. Weighted change is2(5/4)+2(1/2)−19/8−19/8=−5/4. Double-counting subsidy as an additional real cost would incorrectly lower the resource measure by2; omitting its financing would incorrectly improve household totals by2.

4. Full policy comparison and different objectives

Let Wₚₛ=ΣωᵢΔcᵢ. For each uniformly feasible policy pcompute E[Wₚ]=ΣπₛWₚₛand E[Gₚ]=ΣπₛΣΔcᵢ. The state frontiers Mₛ=maxₚWₚₛare (0,0,11/4,1,27/4,5). The outside policy uniquely attains bothθ1frontiers; policy(2,0,1,1)uniquely attains all fourθ2/θ3frontiers. Every other feasible policy is checked against the same frontier; an infeasible policy never establishes a benchmark.

The unique expected-weighted maximizer is(1,0,1,1), with E[W]=3/16and expected resource loss5/4. It funds one slot, no fee, subsidy one and abatement. Its state weighted values are (-3/8,-5/4,13/8,3/4,29/8,11/4). Multiplication by the six stated probabilities gives3/16. At the baseline mean effect3/2and mean damage3, its expected group changes are(23/8,−23/16,−43/32,−43/32). Their sum is−5/4and their weighted sum is3/16; the gains accrue to the highest-priority group, while even P2loses.

The unique expected-resource maximizer is no program, with zero gain. In this model the distributional weight can favor a program that reduces total goods. That is an explicit normative tradeoff, not a computational inconsistency or a theorem that redistribution is costless. The comparison record is (expected weighted optimum,its resource gain,expected resource optimum,robust-policy expected weighted)=(3/16,-5/4,0,-1/8). Full output rows make the global claim auditable; presenting only these three candidates would not by itself prove optimality over37actions.

5. Regret protects against a different error

Define rₚₛ=Mₛ−Wₚₛ≥0and Rₚ=maxₛrₚₛ. The unique minimizer is(2,0,1,1), with regrets (5/4,3,0,0,0,0)and worst regret3. The expected choice(1,0,1,1)has regrets(3/8,5/4,9/8,1/4,25/8,9/4), so its worst regret25/8exceeds3. No program has worst regret27/4. Thus (outside,expected choice,robust choice)=(27/4,25/8,3). The robust program has expected weighted change−1/8under the supplied probabilities. A regret criterion can select a negative-expectation action when that action avoids sufficiently large state-specific opportunities forgone.

Globality is elementary but conditional: the Cartesian policy constructor generates every allowed positive-capacity tuple exactly once plus the outside tuple. The funding and all-state feasibility filters implement the stated constraints. Every survivor's unique allocation and exact accounts are evaluated in every state. Taking finite maxima and then a minimum therefore examines the entire admissible domain. Report every equal minimizer before applying lexicographic selection; this instance has one. Exact fractions avoid numerical near-ties. No claim extends to continuous capacities, different fees, adaptive state-contingent policy or lotteries.

A lottery chosen before the state changes feasible payoffs to convex combinations, and worst regret becomes a piecewise-linear function of lottery probabilities. It can improve the deterministic value; the deterministic optimum does not solve that enlarged problem. Likewiseθvalues between the supplied grid points can cross participation thresholds and need separate analysis. Neither a finite robust result nor a heldout fit authorizes quietly enlarging its scope.

6. Exact forecast switches

For each policy, average the two damage-state payoffs atθ1to get Aₚ, and subtract that average from the correspondingθ3average to get Bₚ. Then forecast value is Aₚ+Bₚq. A policy is optimal exactly where(Aₚ−Aⱼ)+(Bₚ−Bⱼ)q≥0for every feasible competitorjand0≤q≤1. A positive slope difference yields a lower bound onq, a negative one an upper bound, and a zero slope requires a nonnegative intercept difference. Intersecting all these closed half-intervals gives the full support set, including singleton ties. This is a necessary-and-sufficient global certificate.

Only three policies have nonempty support intervals: no program has0on[0,13/64];(1,0,1,1)has−13/16+4qon[13/64,21/64]; and(2,0,1,1)has−17/8+8qon[21/64,1]. Neighboring policies tie at each shared endpoint; elsewhere the maximizer is unique. The breakpoint record is (first switch,second switch,baseline mean-equivalent q)=(13/64,21/64,1/4). All other28uniformly feasible policies have empty support intervals.

The baseline effect distribution has mean3/2, equal to the two-endpoint distribution atq1/4. This lies strictly inside the one-slot interval and reproduces its optimal choice. This agreement follows from the computed upper envelope and these candidates' affine effect payoffs, not from a blanket mean-sufficiency theorem. Other policies have participation thresholds and nonlinear payoff responses; the forecasts differ in their probability onθ2, and a regret calculation uses support rather than a mean. Preserve those distinctions when transporting this sensitivity result.

7. Reproduction and a conditional recommendation

The reference API is run(data): it returns strict JSON-compatible values without writing, printing or mutating data. Integers and rational strings preserve exact fractions. The reader CLI quietly writes its neighboring output, or accepts explicit input and output paths. It rejects direct, resolved, symlink and existing-hardlink aliases of input, code, README or manifest before writing. The manifest binds the other four downloadable payloads; it is not a signature or a guarantee of scientific correctness. Compare its hashes before running and use the output's complete rows to reconstruct a policy independently.

A complete audit demonstrates the actual isolated execution, verifies every protected byte after an attempted alias write, and shows an unfunded policy's reserve-limit diagnostic. Check total mass, positive normalized state weights, shares and nonnegative consumption; do not renormalize malformed inputs silently. The reference uses exact rational arithmetic, so exact fields have zero tolerance. If a learner uses floating point, require account and payoff residuals at most10⁻⁹and separate tie logic from arbitrary rounding; the exact benchmark resolves this instance's ties. Successful code execution alone is insufficient: a checker that imports the same payoff function as its sole oracle could repeat the same error.

An acceptable memo might select the one-slot policy under the stated expected weighted objective, while disclosing its expected resource loss and losses for nonpriority groups. A different memo may select no program under unweighted resources or two slots under deterministic minimax regret. Full credit requires matching the recommendation to the declared objective and correctly reporting all comparisons; it does not require a preferred political viewpoint. The two-slot policy needs reserve9, which is within10but would fail a tighter reserve cap8unless redesigned.

Possible omitted mechanisms include capacity rents and migration induced by a scaled program, or administrator discretion that changes access and leakage. The first needs credible supply/migration response evidence and a larger equilibrium model; the second needs verified eligibility, expenditure tracing and incentive analysis. A prespecified revision could suspend expansion if a randomized offer study, with spillover measurement, places the causal gain below the range making the selected program preferable after actual resource costs, or if verified financing cannot meet the initial reserve. A trial would need its own budget and assignment design; no free pilot is embedded here. Observational fit, a favorable weighted calculation and affordability within this toy treasury do not establish actual legal authority, administrative capacity or democratic legitimacy.

Score the displayed criteria once, not again under neighboring tasks. Method connections and evidence limits

Besley and Persson’s state-capacity manuscript provides bounded context for institutional investments constraining later choices. The fixed reserve rule here is original and does not reproduce their model. MIT’s instrument-choice lecture motivates distinguishing environmental resources and policy instruments; no real emissions calibration is imported. The Chetty–Hendren–Katz author manuscript provides design context for offers, selection and treatment interpretation. The four observational means here are invented and are not a replication of that experiment.

Source scope reuses the accepted chapters' actual bounded primary-text inspections with original inspector attribution. No new full-document or rendered inspection is claimed. All37policies, moments, proofs, seven tasks and benchmark values were created for this project. For delayed transfer, lower the reserve cap to8or allow policy lotteries; first state which previous certificate fails, then solve the changed feasible problem. A reproducible answer that preserves the objective and evidence boundary is the target.

Required policy dossier — connect the laboratory to evidence and institutional history

The numerical laboratory establishes conditional decisions. Completing this volume's project also requires a literature map, an institutional history, a causal-evidence assessment, a distributional account and an implementation memo. Submit this dossier with the seven laboratory tasks. The laboratory retains its 100-point rubric; this companion has a separate 40-point rubric. Pass both: at least 85/100 with the stated laboratory domain floors, and at least 34/40 with no dossier dimension below 6/8, plus correction of every critical integrity or identification error. Scores cannot compensate across the two components. These are authored study thresholds, not externally calibrated standards. Allow another 6–8 hours, open resources, after completing the laboratory.

Use the United States Moving to Opportunity housing experiment as the historical evidence case. The question is deliberately narrower than whether neighborhoods matter: What can an offer of housing assistance establish about outcomes for participating families, and what additional evidence would a new local opportunity program require? The laboratory's service-linked work program is a different intervention. Its four groups, costs, effect grid, forecasts and welfare weights remain synthetic. Historical housing evidence does not calibrate those inputs. A complete answer must identify this mismatch rather than attach a real citation to invented quantities.

The four source cards below are sufficient for the bounded assessment. Their claims and access limits are supplied here so that the dossier remains usable offline. Links allow further primary-source reading when connected. No restricted household records are provided or required. Do not present this exercise as a replication of an empirical paper. For a quantitative empirical extension, first obtain lawful access, a data dictionary, the exact specification and a reproducible output; unavailable evidence should be recorded as unavailable.

All four records were inspected as HTML text on 16 October 2026. D3 is an author summary and publication record, not a fresh full-paper replication; D2 is an official announcement, not the entire report. The dossier's historical boundary ends with the identified 2016 article. It makes no claim about current voucher rules, present eligibility, current funding or a city's legal authority.

Draw a directed map with the MTO assignment cohort as the shared ancestor. D1 describes early delivery; D2 summarizes a later evaluation; D3 analyzes later child outcomes from the same experiment; D4 describes the program and subsequent data-linkage context. Four documents therefore do not constitute four independent randomized experiments. Label edges as “same cohort,” “later observation,” or “institutional description,” rather than counting all positive statements as independent confirmations.

Five dossier tasks

  1. Literature map and claim ledger. Create one row for each source: author/institution, document date or vintage, population, intervention, comparison, outcome horizon, design, admissible claim and unresolved limitation. Mark unavailable details explicitly. Draw the dependency map and classify two statements as institutional description, causal interpretation or normative judgment. Explain why repeated use of one experiment does not provide independent replication.
  2. Institutional history. Build a timeline separating assignment, offer, counseling, completed move, outcome measurement and publication. Include the verified dated milestones supplied in the cards, while leaving family-specific events undated. Name the delivery actors and one bottleneck supported by the institutional description. Explain why a later child-outcome finding need not logically contradict an earlier adult-outcome finding. Give one claim the short source cards cannot settle.
  3. Causal evidence. Define an intention-to-treat estimand for one voucher-offer comparison, and distinguish it from an effect among movers. State the observation and assignment assumptions required for identification. Derive the binary instrumental-variable ratio under additional assumptions, and explain why it need not isolate neighborhood poverty from counseling or other bundled services. List the population, outcome, horizon and interference conditions needed before transporting any conclusion to the local work-service laboratory.
  4. Distribution and a decision. Select either expected weighted welfare, expected resources or deterministic minimax regret in the laboratory. Report its policy, objective value, funding and who may lose. Contrast its decision assumptions with what the historical cards actually establish. Then propose a bounded real-program decision memo: state the target group, outside option, budget information still needed, an implementer and a measurable revision trigger. “Defer scale-up while resolving a specified missing fact” is a legitimate decision; an invented benefit-cost ratio is not.
  5. Feasible implementation and adversarial handoff. Supply a responsibility and evidence table for authorization, recruitment, counseling or service delivery, payments, outcome follow-up and complaints. Separate historical actors from proposed roles. Set a funded pilot stage gate without inventing legal permission or treating future benefits as current cash. Write a 150-word skeptical referee note on your own recommendation and a response identifying what you changed or still cannot establish. Preserve a source/version log and identify what a reader can reproduce offline.
Instructor guide, illustrative answers and grading boundaries

1. Build a map of claims, not a vote count

A complete ledger records D1 as a March 1996 administrative account with implementation activity as its object; its supplied text supports delivery processes, not an income treatment effect. D2 is a November 2011 official summary of evaluation outcomes; exact coefficients and uncertainty are “not supplied.” D3 is an author research summary identifying a 2016 article and later childhood outcomes; the publication year must not be mistaken for assignment year. D4 provides program chronology and assignment-group descriptions; its separate Family Options discussion is outside this case. State sample size only if separately verified at the intended precision; it is unnecessary for this assessment.

The dependency graph has one experiment feeding several records. Agreement among its publications can increase coherence, but common participants, assignment and measurement histories create dependence. A statement about an agency's counseling partners is institutional description. A difference attributed to randomized offer assignment is a causal interpretation requiring an estimand and valid observation. Giving extra welfare weight to low-income groups is a normative judgment. Publication by a respected institution does not collapse these categories.

Award 2 points for four identifiable source/vintage rows; 2 for explicit unavailable fields and admissible claims; 2 for a correct shared-cohort graph; 2 for the classifications and replication distinction.

2. Establish the sequence before telling a success story

A valid skeleton is: 1994–1998 assignment window; March 1996 implementation report, inside that window; follow-up through 2010 and the November 2011 evaluation announcement; later child-outcome analysis identified as the 2016 article. The cards do not give each household's counseling dates, move date or observation date. Those belong in separate event columns marked unknown, not filled with the publication date. Some early administrative observations were made while later families were still entering the experiment, so a single common “before” date would erase the program's staggered history.

HUD's 1996 account supplies public housing agencies and nonprofit counseling organizations as delivery actors. Its sequence from outreach through applications and enrollment motivates a proposed recruitment or delivery-capacity bottleneck, but does not estimate which stage caused an outcome. A new dossier should seek dated waiting-list, offer, counseling and lease records to test such a hypothesis. These records would also help distinguish eligibility, offer and take-up; they would not themselves randomize take-up.

An earlier adult economic-outcome result and a later childhood-exposure result concern different ages and potentially different horizons. They can both be true. A careful comparison holds outcome, sample and follow-up fixed before calling results contradictory. The short cards cannot establish the precise size, uncertainty or mechanism of either effect; nor do they show that a particular counselor caused a household to move. An evidence gap is an appropriate conclusion.

Award 2 for correctly ordered verified milestones; 2 for distinct undated household events; 2 for actors plus a testable rather than asserted bottleneck; 2 for the age/horizon reconciliation and one explicit unresolved claim.

3. An offer is a defined intervention

For a chosen pair of assignment arms, let Z be the randomized offer, Y(z) the outcome at a prespecified horizon under that assignment, and D(z) a precisely defined binary take-up event. The intention-to-treat target is E[Y(1)−Y(0)] in the eligible randomized population. Under assignment independence, consistency, positive assignment probabilities and valid observation of that population, it equals E[Y|Z=1]−E[Y|Z=0]. Differential loss to follow-up, failed linkage or outcome definitions that depend on assignment require additional treatment; random assignment alone does not repair them. If site-specific assignment probabilities differ, compare within design strata and aggregate with declared target weights.

To interpret the offer as an instrument for D, additionally assume exclusion of direct offer effects, no defiers D(1)≥D(0), a positive first stage, and a coherent treatment version and interference definition. Write Y=Y(0)+D[Y(1)−Y(0)] using treatment-indexed potential outcomes under exclusion. Subtract assignment-arm expectations. The reduced form is E[(D(1)−D(0))(Y(1)−Y(0))]; under monotonicity it equals the complier share times the complier average effect. The first stage E[D|Z=1]−E[D|Z=0] is that share. Their ratio identifies the complier effect, not automatically the effect on all movers or all eligible families. In this paragraph Y(d) is treatment-indexed; it differs from the assignment-indexed Y(z) above.

The derivation is a conditional identification argument, not a claim that every assumption holds for an MTO mechanism. If assignment changes counseling, expectations or assistance before a move, exclusion for a variable defined merely as “moved” can fail. Even a valid effect of a bundled move intervention need not identify the isolated effect of neighborhood poverty. A continuous exposure measure, multiple assignment arms or several move types needs its own estimand and assumptions.

Transport to the laboratory would require comparable populations and take-up constraints, comparable interventions and outside options, measured outcomes that map to its resource objective, a justified horizon and price conversion, and an interference/scaling model. None is supplied by fitting the laboratory's four invented means. The laboratory sensitivity restriction on selection, finite state weights and group welfare weights remain assumptions. A disciplined answer refuses to replace θ with an unverified housing estimate.

Award 2 for the ITT target and assignment/observation conditions; 2 for the reduced-form/first-stage derivation; 2 for the complier and bundled-treatment limits; 2 for explicit transport requirements and rejection of false calibration. Treat an unsupported movers-versus-nonmovers causal comparison as a critical error.

4. Carry the decision's losses into the memo

One acceptable laboratory recommendation is capacity one, fee zero, subsidy one and abatement one under expected weighted welfare. Its initial reserve is 1(3+1)+1=5. The supplied probabilities imply weighted gain 3/16 and resource change −5/4. Expected group changes are (23/8,−23/16,−43/32,−43/32); only P1 gains. Their sum is −5/4 and weights (2,2,1,1) give 3/16. Thus the recommendation buys a distributional objective while losing total goods in this model. A proposal that reports only its positive objective omits the central tradeoff.

Two alternative recommendations earn equal credit if argued consistently. Under expected resources, no program uniquely maximizes the objective at zero, with no program levy or model-induced losses. Under deterministic minimax regret, capacity two with the same fee, subsidy and abatement needs reserve 9 and minimizes worst regret at 3, despite expected weighted change −1/8. Its low-effect state already exhibits losers in the laboratory's manual account. These are different objectives, not three estimates of the same empirical welfare effect.

An illustrative real-program memo might propose gathering a costed design for a voluntary offer targeted to a clearly defined eligible group, preserving the current assistance option. It would specify an accountable local delivery organization, seek per-offer and per-completed-service cost records, distinguish up-front cash from discounted future benefits, and require an evaluation protocol before scale-up. It cannot recommend a precise MTO-based subsidy or an actual city's legal action from these cards. A revision trigger could be verified inability to fund promised services or a prespecified adverse outcome boundary; the threshold and monitoring design must be fixed before inspecting results. Health, earnings, family disruption, rents, movers and nonparticipants belong in separate outcome accounts rather than a single unexplained index.

Award 2 for a correct objective/policy/value; 2 for reserve and group/resource accounts; 2 for separating historical evidence from invented calibration; 2 for a bounded decision, outside option and measurable revision trigger.

5. Assign responsibility without inventing authority

A defensible proposed responsibility table assigns: authorization to the relevant public decision-maker, with a dated authority/funding document still required; recruitment to an eligibility team, with an auditable offer log; counseling or service delivery to a contracted provider, with capacity and completion records; payments to a finance officer, with commitments and a cash ledger; follow-up to an evaluation team, with consent, data permissions and an attrition plan; complaints to an identifiable review channel, with resolution records. These are proposed functions. Only the historical agencies and counseling organizations named in D1 are source-supported actors; the cards do not establish any current jurisdiction's powers.

The first stage gate is a verified budget and feasible delivery plan. Specify which commitments can be made before enrollment, the reserve required under low take-up and high take-up, and who may stop new offers while honoring outstanding obligations. The second is a feasible evaluation with assignment and outcome definitions, protected data handling, funding for follow-up and a declared stopping rule. The third is a documented review of benefits, losses and implementation against that protocol. A future earnings projection is not cash available to pay today's provider. A pilot also consumes resources and can change behavior; it is not free information.

An illustrative skeptical note is: “The preferred numerical policy depends on assumed forecasts, a privileged access order and an explicitly unequal welfare criterion. Historical housing offers do not identify the productivity effect of this service. The proposed recruitment process could exclude the people with the largest gains, and the budget does not yet price follow-up. The memo should retain the current outside option and postpone irrevocable expansion until it has a costed delivery protocol and a defensible comparison.” A good response accepts the valid limits, adds follow-up costs and a recruitment audit, and states what remains unknown. It need not capitulate to an unsupported criticism or pretend that qualitative risks have been quantified.

The source log should retain URLs, document vintages, access dates, the bounded claims actually inspected and the difference between author summaries and full reports. Offline readers can reproduce the synthetic laboratory, inspect the provided claim cards, recompute the hypothetical accounts and evaluate the written identification argument. They cannot reproduce confidential empirical estimates from this package. That boundary is part of the deliverable.

Award 2 for six assigned functions with evidence requirements; 2 for funded stage gates and treatment of obligations; 2 for a substantive skeptical note and responsive revision; 2 for the source/version log and honest reproduction boundary.

Defense and delayed transfer

In an oral defense, ask the learner to replace a randomized offer with voluntary enrollment while holding the observed outcome gap fixed. A satisfactory answer withdraws the random-assignment interpretation, names selection into enrollment and proposes a credible design or explicit sensitivity analysis. Then change the lab reserve ceiling from 10 to 8: the two-slot minimax policy's reserve 9 fails, so its old optimality certificate no longer applies. The correct next step is to re-enumerate the changed feasible set, not finance the gap with hoped-for benefits. Two weeks later, require a new source card from a different policy setting and a short explanation of which treatment, population and institutional assumptions do or do not transfer.

Oral transfer and teach-back

Answer all five prompts aloud after written remediation, allowing about5minutes each plus follow-up questions. Each is4points; require17/20and at least3perdomain. Explain a changed premise without reading a stored answer. Timing and cutoffs are uncalibrated.

  1. Voting is not a welfare theorem. Three voters choose a nonnegative public good G. Each gets benefit aiG with a=(1,2,5) and pays G²/2; total production cost is3G²/2. Derive the majority winner and aggregate-surplus optimum, prove their globality, and identify what compensation or voting reform would need to specify.
  2. A tariff receipt has a foreign counterparty. A small country faces world price4, demand10−p and supply p−2, both nonnegative on the relevant range. Apply a tariff1 and compare domestic consumer surplus, producer surplus and government receipts with free trade. Imports are paid by exporting the numeraire; tariff receipts are rebated without changing marginal incentives. Explain the world-price-taking limitation.
  3. An archive copy is not independent evidence. Two exhaustive historical mechanisms have equal prior probabilities. An archival record occurs with likelihood3/5 under A and1/5 under B. Compute the posterior for A. A later source exactly copies that record. Compare the proper update with incorrectly treating the copy as an independent equally informative record. What evidence would actually help discriminate?
  4. Distinguish a belief from a rewarded report. A person believes a binary event has probability4/5. The score is S=1−(q−Y)². Prove expected-money truthfulness and compare expected scores at q=4/5 and1/2. Then use an independent lottery that pays a high rather than low prize with probability S, but suppose the utility gain from that high prize is one in event1 and two in event0. Find the optimal report and explain the failure.
  5. Name whose housing gain is measured. A neighborhood improvement gives two tenants consumption-equivalent benefits6and2 and uses resources4, financed by levies2on each tenant. The first tenant also pays an additional rent3 to an absentee owner; the second rent is fixed. Compute the gains of both tenants and the owner, aggregate welfare, and the result if the social evaluator gives the first tenant weight2 and everyone else weight1. State what changes if rents or population are endogenous.
Complete answers and additive scoring

  1. Each utility aiG−G²/2 is strictly concave with ideal ai. Single-peakedness gives median ideal2 as the Condorcet winner: against a lower G, the two voters with ideals2and5 prefer2; against a higher G, those with ideals1and2 prefer2. Aggregate surplus is8G−3G²/2, globally maximized at8/3. Its values are (2,8/3,10,32/3,2/3), listing winner,planner,values and gain. The change need not benefit every voter under the stated tax shares. A compensation proposal needs actual transfers, a payer and a rule preserving incentives; calling the sum larger does not change the vote.

    Rubric (4 points). Individual/global preferences1; majority proof1; planner/value1; distribution/institution1. Study route: v15-c06.

  2. Free trade gives demand6,supply2,imports4, consumer surplus18 and producer surplus2. The tariff gives price5,demand5,supply3,imports2, consumer surplus25/2, producer surplus9/2 and receipts2. Domestic welfare falls from20 to19, so (6,2,4,5,3,2,20,19,1). Foreign suppliers receive8 numeraire after the tariff, domestic government2, and domestic producers15; consumers spend25. The additional domestic resources cost must be counted, while tariff payments cancel against rebates. A large country could affect the foreign price; this problem deliberately excludes that terms-of-trade mechanism and retaliation.

    Rubric (4 points). Equilibrium quantities1; surplus/receipt calculation1; counterpart/resource account1; welfare and scope1. Study route: v15-c05.

  3. Prior odds1 become likelihood odds3, giving posterior3/4. Conditional on the observed record, its deterministic copy has probabilityone under either mechanism, so it adds no likelihood information. False independence multiplies by3 again, giving9/10. Thus (3/4,3/4,9/10). A genuinely new record helps only when its conditional likelihood differs between the mechanisms after existing evidence. A contemporaneous alternative archive with understood preservation and access rules might do so; chronological lateness alone is not independence. The two-mechanism model may omit joint explanations.

    Rubric (4 points). Bayes odds1; dependency1; false update1; discriminating evidence/scope1. Study route: v15-c07.

  4. Completing the square gives E[S]=1−p(1−p)−(q−p)², uniquely maximized atq=p on[0,1]. At the two reports expected scores are21/25 and3/4, a gap9/100. With event-dependent prize gains the relevant objective is(4/5)S(q,1)+(2/5)S(q,0), up to a q-independent term. Its derivative is(8/5)(1−q)−(4/5)q, giving q=2/3; the second derivative is negative. (21/25,3/4,9/100,2/3). Binarization removes curvature over fixed prizes only under state-independent utility differences and understood independent randomization. The reporting distortion does not establish an incorrect belief. The sponsor must reserve the high monetary prize in every state.

    Rubric (4 points). Completed square/globality1; score gap1; weighted optimum1; violated assumption/funding1. Study route: v15-c08.

  5. Gains are6−2−3=1,2−2=0,and3. Total4 equals gross amenity8 minus resources4. The weighted value is2·1+0+3=5. Thus (1,0,3,4,5). Rent is a transfer within the stated welfare boundary; excluding the absentee owner changes that boundary, not the physical resource calculation. Doubling a tenant’s weight is a normative choice. With endogenous migration, rents and occupancy must satisfy equilibrium and capacity, and original residents must be distinguished from whoever lives there afterward. Fixed incomes must cover rent and levies; these stipulated transfers alone do not establish a feasible housing equilibrium.

    Rubric (4 points). Individual gains1; aggregate cancellation1; weights1; ownership/population/feasibility1. Study route: v15-c11.

Delayed retention

Return after one to two weeks, then revisit weak domains after a month. Allow150minutes without notes or code, extending time when necessary to complete a proof. Each task is10points; require43/50and at least8perdomain, with every critical error repaired. These changed problems emphasize transfer rather than memorized chapter parameters.

  1. Two funded tax equilibria. A unit mass of identical price-taking workers has utility c−L² plus a public-service benefit6. Gross wage is8 and c=(8−t)L; each worker takes public service and tax t as given. Government must raise6 to buy6 units of real public-service inputs. Taxes satisfy0≤t≤8. Derive labor supply and every balanced-budget tax. Compare aggregate welfare and prove which funded policy is better.
  2. Entry is not automatically efficient. Identical Cournot firms face p=20−Q, marginal cost4 and fixed real entry cost9. An active firm chooses nonnegative output taking rivals fixed. Find the symmetric equilibrium for nfirms, the free-entry number using nonnegative incumbent profit and no profitable additional entrant, and welfare at n=1,2 and the free-entry count. A planner can choose output and the number of active plants. Find its optimum and explain the difference.
  3. Poverty objectives and historical sensitivity. Two incomes are1and3, poverty line4, and a transfer budget2 must be fully distributed without making either income exceed4. Find the allocation minimizing the mean squared normalized poverty gap, and contrast a headcount-minimizing allocation. Then a historical policy study reports DiD3. Let an untreated trend difference δlie in[−1/2,1/2] and the comparison group’s treatment spillover s in[0,1], with identity DiD=τ+δ−s. Derive the sharp effect interval and explain why it does not identify which poverty objective was achieved.
  4. Insurance, voting and care are separate constraints. A unit mass of applicants has equal shares of loss probabilities1/5and4/5, wealth9, loss8 and square-root utility. Insurers can offer only a common full-insurance premium, have zero costs beyond claims, and applicants buy at indifference. Find willingness to pay, the competitive positive-coverage zero-profit equilibrium and the smallest uniform per-person outside subsidy supporting a full pool. Three outside voters would each pay one third of the total subsidy; their gross benefits are0,1/2,2. Does majority voting approve? Separately, an insured patient chooses care q∈[0,5] with benefit5q−q²/2, real costq and patient cost share1/2. Find private and efficient q and the social loss, with the insurer paying the other half.
  5. Value a feasible pilot, not an unfunded option. Policies0,A,B yield net social surpluses(0,0),(8,−2),(3,4) in states H,L. The prior is1/2. Implementation cash costs are0,4,2, already deducted in those net payoffs; available reserve is initially5. A pilot costs1 now and produces a binary signal with Pr(+|H)=Pr(−|L)=3/4. Choose the final policy after seeing it; unused reserve is retained. Compute the best no-pilot policy, every policy’s worst regret, the best contingent pilot rule and its net gain, and perfect-information value as an upper bound. Then reduce reserve to4 and reoptimize pilot versus no pilot. Give a finite monitoring rule for five proposed later tests with total false-alarm probability at most5%, without assuming independence.
Complete answers and additive scoring

  1. Strict concavity of(8−t)L−L² onL≥0 gives L=(8−t)/2, including zero at t=8. Revenue t(8−t)/2=6 becomes t²−8t+12=0, with exactly two feasible roots2and6. Labor is3or1. Production8L pays private consumption18or2 and government inputs6. Private consumption minus labor disutility plus benefit6 is15or7. Hence (2,6,3,1,18,2,15,7). The lower tax is strictly better among all funded taxes: the quadratic equation exhausted the feasible set. Total welfare also equals8L−L² because service benefit equals its real input cost; comparing to the undistorted maximum16 shows losses1and9. An atomistic worker takes the service fixed; differentiating its own benefit through total revenue would define another game.

    Rubric (10 points). Global labor2; all revenue roots2; accounts2; welfare2; complete ranking and price-taking scope2. Study route: v15-c01.

  2. For nactive firms the unique symmetric positive solution is q=16/(n+1), p=4+q. Strict concavity of each firm’s quantity payoff validates its best response. Net profit is256/(n+1)²−9. Incumbent viability requires n+1≤16/3; no profitable additional entrant requires n+2≥16/3, so the unique integer count is4. With totalQ=16n/(n+1), aggregate surplus is16Q−Q²/2−9n. At n=1,2,4 this is (87,862/9,2172/25). Four-firm output64/5 and per-firm profit31/25 are (4,64/5,31/25). The next entrant earns256/36−9<0. A planner uses one plant, since extra identical plants add fixed costs without expanding its feasible production set; it chooses Q=16 from strict concavity, earning welfare119. Zero plants yields0, and every n≥2 has the same best variable surplus128 with larger9n cost. (1,16,119). Business stealing can sustain too many plants relative to this unrestricted planner; a planner restricted to Cournot output would be a different comparison.

  3. Let x go to the poorer person and2−x to the other. Feasibility gives1≤x≤2. Remaining gaps are3−x andx−1, so P2=[(3−x)²+(x−1)²]/32. The derivative is(x−2)/8 and the second derivative1/8>0; the global minimum isx=2, leaving incomes3,3 and P2=1/16, but both remain poor. A headcount optimum isx=1, giving2,4 and P0=1/2; both cannot reach4 because that would require4 units. Both allocations have P1=1/4. (2,1/16,1,1/2,1/4) lists squared-gap allocation/value,alternative allocation,headcount and common gap. Rearranging givesτ=3−δ+s, whose sharp endpoints are5/2and9/2. (5/2,9/2). Independent closed sensitivity restrictions attain both corners and every intervening value. A positive mean outcome effect is not a poverty-distribution effect: one needs the outcome definition, population weights, income distribution/counterfactual and credible restrictions on selection/spillovers.

    Rubric (10 points). Feasible transfer set/global derivative2; objectives and values2; headcount proof1; sensitivity bounds/attainability2; identification versus distribution3. Study route: v15-c04.

  4. Uninsured expected utilities are13/5and7/5; reservation premiums are9−169/25=56/25 and9−49/25=176/25. Expected claims are8/5and32/5; full pooling costs4, above low-risk willingness. A premium at or below56/25 attracts both and loses money; between that value and176/25 it attracts only high risks, with zero profit at32/5. Thus high-only coverage is the positive-coverage competitive equilibrium, with mass1/2. The required pool subsidy is4−56/25=44/25, paid per applicant; the common private premium is56/25. (56/25,176/25,32/5,1/2,44/25). Each outsider pays44/75, exceeding the first two voters’ benefits; only the third approves. An economically fundable proposal can fail its political rule. Any alternative coalition needs its own distribution and budget. The patient’s strictly concave net benefit has derivative5−q−1/2, giving q=9/2; social derivative4−q gives q*=4. Surpluses are63/8and8, loss1/8. (9/2,4,63/8,8,1/8,9/4,9/4) adds patient and insurer bills9/4each. Their sum equals resource cost9/2. This second calculation does not alter the first model’s fixed claims without explicitly replacing its insurance technology.

    Rubric (10 points). Reservation values/pool2; equilibrium regions2; funded subsidy/vote2; global care2; resource and model separation2. Study route: v15-c10.

  5. Without the pilot expected surpluses are0,3,7/2, so chooseB. Statewise best values are8,4, yielding worst regrets8,6,5 for0,A,B; minimax regret also selectsB. (0,3,7/2,8,6,5). A beatsB when10p−2≥4−p, orp≥6/11; Bbeats0 at every posterior. Signal probabilities are both1/2, with posterior3/4after+ and1/4after−. The globally optimal contingent rule isAafter+ andBafter−. Conditional expected values are11/2and15/4; averaging yields37/8before pilot cost and29/8after it, a gain1/8over7/2. Its highest cash demand is1+4=5, actually covered. Perfect information gives6before information cost, so its value relative to no pilot is5/2; the imperfect signal’s gross value is9/8, below that bound. (6/11,3/4,1/4,37/8,29/8,1/8,6,5/2,9/8). With reserve4, undertaking the pilot leaves3, makingAinfeasible in both signal states. Balways dominates0, so pilot value is7/2−1=5/2; rejecting the pilot and implementingB yields7/2. (5/2,7/2). A calculation using the previous contingent rule would spend money unavailable after the signal. For five prespecified valid tests, size at most1/100each gives union probability at most5/100by summing marginal rejection probabilities. Specify outcomes, stopping decisions and the family before data; searching repeatedly or changing the family requires a revised guarantee. The stipulated prior and signal law are assumptions, not estimated policy evidence.

    Rubric (10 points). No-pilot and regrets2; posterior/global policy comparison2; net information value2; statewise funding/reoptimization2; valid prespecified monitoring and evidence scope2. Study route: v15-c12.

Remediation and reassessment

Maintain an error ledger containing the exact prompt, your inference, the violated assumption, a corrected derivation and one new problem. Rework the error from a blank page before rereading the solution. A copied correct answer is a learning aid, not a passing attempt.

  • Feasibility or incidence: write individual cash and real-resource accounts, including owners, outsiders, government and every relevant state. Return to chapters1,3,5,9–12.
  • Optimization or equilibrium: specify the full action set, all boundaries, the timing of information, the decision rule and the global proof. Return to chapters2,3,6,8–11.
  • Causal or archival inference: define the estimand, observation law, missingness, interference, selection and the exact restriction that excludes a rival explanation. Return to chapters2,4,5,7,8,10–12and Volume12.
  • Distribution or welfare: distinguish personal incomes, prices, amenities, transfer recipients and real costs; state the social weights and population boundary. Return to chapters1,4,5,8,9,11.
  • Implementation: identify authority as a fact requiring verification, specify capacity, cash reserves, consent and participation, and show a funded revision rule. Return to chapters6and12and the project.

For a failed domain, explain the repair aloud and solve a changed feasible problem before taking the alternate form. Preserve disagreements between defensible welfare criteria. External expert judgment remains necessary for real research and policy advice.

Concept and outcome index

  1. Public economics and taxation: Analyze tax and spending decisions with efficiency and distribution in view.
  2. Labor economics and human capital: Evaluate wage, employment and education mechanisms using credible designs.
  3. Industrial organization and competition: Assess market conduct and competitive policy using models and evidence.
  4. Development, poverty and structural change: Compare poverty-reduction mechanisms and their institutional constraints.
  5. International trade and global production: Analyze firm and worker responses to trade and production networks.
  6. Political economy and institutions: Analyze collective decisions and institutional incentives with defensible identification.
  7. Economic history and historical inference: Use historical evidence to distinguish mechanisms and avoid anachronistic causal claims.
  8. Behavioral and experimental economics: Design and critique evidence about nonstandard preferences and beliefs.
  9. Environmental, energy and climate economics: Evaluate externalities and long-horizon choices under uncertainty.
  10. Health, education and demographic economics: Assess service provision and demographic change through incentives and evidence.
  11. Urban economics, housing and inequality: Analyze spatial decisions and distribution with equilibrium feedback.
  12. Policy synthesis and institutional feasibility: Defend an implementable policy with evidence, uncertainty and distributional consequences.

Each written form maps all twelve chapter outcomes to bounded tasks. This does not mean that twenty subparts test every issue in every field. The project adds implementation, and the oral and retention tasks test changed assumptions. Full field expertise requires deeper literature, evidence and repeated expert evaluation.

Volume synthesis

A field supplies substantive mechanisms and institutions; it does not suspend the common requirements of choice, equilibrium, accounting and identification. Labor, education and health policies change behavior. Market structure and trade redistribute gains. Historical records have selection and dependence. Environmental and spatial effects cross the boundary of a private transaction. Political approval and administrative capacity can prevent a positive-surplus proposal from being implemented.

Carry three outputs into the next stage: an explicit model with global reasoning and named payers; an evidence map separating measured, assumed and unidentified objects; and a decision rule tied to resources, uncertainty and revision. The integrated policy/investment case brings these together with valuation. Specialization and original research requires a scoped question and new defensible contribution, followed by teaching and leadership portfolios whose learner-specific achievements cannot be supplied by a textbook.

Sources and scope

All questions, parameter values, derivations and grading rules are original. Linked chapters supply the underlying methods and their primary-source routes. Three retained method references are the MIT environmental instrument-choice lecture, Fehr and Schmidt’s social-preference paper, and Allcott’s resource-economics notes. The source record reuses their actual bounded prior inspections; this package asserts no new complete-document or image review and copies no source examination. Conditional models and internal review cannot substitute for actual institutional evidence or independent human assessment.
